title: PackClient
subtitle: Reverse Engineering a Modular RAT Framework
author: Ivan Immanuel Shaji

sections.title: From Launcher to recovered Core
sections.deck: One chain connects the signed host, injected Launcher, PLK1 delivery, recovered Core, persistence, and live C2 traffic.

blocks.text:
This research follows one PackClient build from its signed host and sideloaded carrier into a suspended 32-bit surrogate, the injected Donut package, Launcher delivery, and the recovered Core.

| Area | Result |
|---|---|
| Launcher | Recovered framing, authentication, PLK1/cache, active-session, and `1RCP` contracts |
| Core | Reconstructed a 985,088-byte `PackClientCore.dll` directly from historical PLK1 traffic and mapped its exports, configuration, plugin interfaces, commands, and screenshot producer |
| Historical traffic | Reassembled `PLH1 -> PLC1 -> PLA1 -> PLK1`, followed by bidirectional Core traffic and 15 `PV10` JPEG frames |
| Persistence | Distinguished the normal full-EXE path from the broken task produced when a sandbox invoked the carrier DLL directly through `rundll32.exe` |

The Launcher's raw-BGRX `1RCP` worker and the Core's GDI/WIC `PV10` producer are separate recovered paths. No component linking them was found, and no plugin binary was present in the available traffic, memory, or cache material. The [PackClient Core analysis](references/core-analysis.html) develops those findings, while [Samples and provenance](references/evidence.html) lists the complete file identities.

sections.title: The signed-host execution chain
sections.deck: The signed host loads a colocated carrier, which starts an embedded Donut package inside a suspended 32-bit surrogate.

blocks.text: The July 2026 Tax Notice lineage places a signed NV Access/NVDA executable beside a malicious `nvdaHelperRemote.dll`. Because the host imports the helper by bare filename, the colocated carrier satisfies the import. At host RVA `0x1004`, the executable calls `nvdaHelperRemote.dll!injection_initialize` through IAT slot `0xF268`. [Samples and provenance](references/evidence.html) identifies the studied host and carrier; the legitimate library layout is described in the [NVDA helper documentation](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/blob/master/nvdaHelper/readme.md).

The installed directory preserves the signed host and its colocated carrier as a pair. The same chain creates a suspended `SysWOW64\svchost.exe`, writes the embedded package into that process, changes its primary-thread context, and resumes execution.

The injected call-over-data package contains a Donut instance and embedded executable A. Four bytes of terminal glue recover the instance pointer from the opening `CALL`; the next 11,647 bytes exactly match Donut `LOADER_EXE_X86` from revision `47758d787209dd1744f58c140102ac91b649df16`, followed by 23 zero bytes. Donut maps A, and A maps `PackClientLauncher.exe` B. The complete package layout appears in the [Launcher architecture](references/launcher-architecture.html).

Across twelve July and August Triage tasks, the protected allocation is 417,792 bytes and has SHA-256 `E49581067CC2AA5ABD09C8DF42D6FBD87CB064A9363FE8B52D8369FD1C51FFE5`. It contains a 415,071-byte logical record; the additional 2,721 allocation bytes remain unexplained. These are distinct objects, so their hashes are not interchangeable. One task records 53 write-labelled events into PID 844 at `0x00440000`, followed by `SetThreadContext` on primary thread 4600. This sequence supports thread execution hijacking (`T1055.003`), not classic process hollowing or remote-thread creation. The carrier's precise write call site and the instruction pointer installed by `SetThreadContext` remain unresolved. See the [Launcher architecture](references/launcher-architecture.html) for the carrier and A-to-B mapping details.

Launcher B provides transport, PLK1 delivery and caching, active-session handoff, and an early screenshot-worker mode. Once PLK1 completes, the recovered Core supplies the wider command set and the `PV10` screenshot path seen in historical traffic.

| Object | Recorded size | Identity anchor |
|---|---:|---|
| Tax Notice host | 120,984 bytes | SHA-256 begins `93DD8B7B393289F8` |
| Sideload carrier | 455,527 bytes | SHA-256 begins `7295090C2CB63EBC` |
| Reconstructed Launcher B | 271,872-byte PE32 executable | SHA-256 begins `46B34789196733FA` |
| Recovered Core | 985,088-byte PE32 DLL | SHA-256 begins `4DE6EF8647FB4B59` |

The [sample and object table](references/evidence.html#artifact-identities) lists the complete hashes.

sections.title: Launcher screenshot worker
sections.deck: An early command-line branch turns Launcher B into a local screenshot worker with a compact 20-byte protocol.

blocks.text:
The worker is selected by an early argument-dispatch branch, before the later active-session/Core path. The interface is `/scr_cap_worker <endpoint-utf8> [monitor-index]`. Its body runs in the already launched process and inherits that process’s token, session and environment. The wrapper exits after the worker returns; the later token-based launch path cannot be used to infer the worker’s original security context. The [screenshot worker analysis](references/screenshot-ipc.html) traces this activation path.

The endpoint argument is converted to UTF-16 and passed to `CreateFileW` with read/write access, no sharing and `OPEN_EXISTING`. There is one open attempt. The recovered path contains no endpoint creator, named-pipe server, wait-for-pipe loop or peer authentication. A named pipe is strongly supported by context, but the argument’s namespace is not recovered; the API itself also accepts other paths. Its endpoint handling is documented with the rest of the [screenshot worker interface](references/screenshot-ipc.html).

After the first successful capture, the worker emits READY. It then accumulates exactly 20 command bytes, checks the magic and dispatches the request type. Correct-magic types other than 3 and 5 are ignored. Bad magic, a failed read or a zero-byte read ends the command loop without a protocol reply.

The header is five little-endian DWORDs. The bytes `31 52 43 50` spell `1RCP`; as a DWORD the magic is `0x50435231`.

A normal exchange follows `1 → 3 → 2 → 5`: the worker announces READY, the peer requests a capture, the worker returns the frame, and the peer eventually exits.

| Type | Direction | Meaning | Dimensions and payload |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Worker → peer | READY | Captured width and height; payload length zero |
| 3 | Peer → worker | Recapture | Request DWORDs 2–4 are ignored |
| 2 | Worker → peer | Frame response | Width, height and following pixel-byte length |
| 5 | Peer → worker | Exit | Request DWORDs 2–4 are ignored; no reply |

Zero-filled request fields are a synthetic test convention, not a worker requirement. The command loop always reads the next 20-byte header and does not consume extra bytes according to the final DWORD. Worker process exit codes are separate from protocol message types.

The selected monitor supplies positive width and height. The DIB uses 32-bit `BI_RGB` with a negative height, producing top-down rows. Each pixel is blue, green, red and an unused fourth byte; meaningful alpha is not established. Stride is `width × 4`, with no additional per-row padding. The expected payload is `width × height × 4`; the IA-32 reconstruction found no separate arithmetic overflow guard. The actual response length is taken from the framebuffer vector’s end-minus-begin distance. The complete field and pixel layout appears in the [screenshot worker analysis](references/screenshot-ipc.html).

Within Launcher B, the pixel path ends at `WriteFile` on the supplied endpoint. No call or data edge carries those pixels into Winsock, PLK1, the encrypted transport, or a JPEG/PV10 conversion path. An external peer could transform or forward the pixels, but that component was not recovered. See the [screenshot worker analysis](references/screenshot-ipc.html) for the complete path.

When this mode is not selected, Launcher B continues into the network framing and authentication path described next.

sections.title: Launcher transport and authentication
sections.deck: Launcher B frames, authenticates, and can decrypt traffic before the Core is loaded; historical captures preserve the plaintext handshake and delivery path.

blocks.text:
The outer frame starts with a little-endian word formed by `0x5A400000 | body_length`. The receiver checks `(frame_word >> 22) == 0x169`, bounds the nonzero body at `0x3FFFFF`, reads it exactly, and requires at least four bytes for the type. Thus `24 00 40 5A` means a 36-byte body and a 40-byte total frame. The complete byte layout is documented in the [Launcher protocol](references/launcher-protocol.html).

| Offset | Bytes | Outer-frame meaning |
|---:|---:|---|
| `0x00` | 4 | Prefix combined with body length |
| `0x04` | 4 | Little-endian type DWORD, part of the body |
| `0x08` | Variable | Payload; body length minus four |

B sends PLH1 and PLA1 in plaintext type `0x15`. Its first framed receive accepts PLC1 either directly in type `0x15` or through an authenticated outer `0x16` envelope with inner type `0x15`, provided the envelope keys are initialized. This receive precedes Core loading. PLH1 is a 32-byte client hello; PLC1 is the 24-byte server challenge; PLA1 is the 40-byte client authentication object. PLH1 includes version 1, an unresolved word set to `0x20`, fixed fields, a tick count and the process ID. PLC1 contributes a 16-byte challenge at offsets `0x08..0x17`; challenge generation lives in the server.

PLA1 uses HMAC-SHA-256 over exactly **42 bytes**, rather than the complete hello and challenge:

```text
PLH1[0x10:0x20]  // 16 bytes
|| PLC1[0x08:0x18]  // 16 bytes
|| PLH1[0x0C:0x10]  //  4 bytes
|| PLH1[0x06:0x08]  //  2 bytes
|| "PLK1"          //  4 bytes
```

The PSK comes from `PACK_LAUNCH_PSK`; missing or empty values select the 19-byte fallback `pack-launch-dev-psk`. After sending PLA1, the recovered function does not wait for a separate authentication acknowledgement. The July captures confirm the plaintext `PLH1 → PLC1 → PLA1` sequence. The [historical traffic record](references/evidence.html) preserves the successful exchange.

### Optional encrypted receive

Type `0x16` is an inbound encrypted envelope. In this B image, the send path constructs only type `0x15`. The envelope carries a version byte, 16-byte IV, four-byte **big-endian** ciphertext length, ciphertext, and a 32-byte HMAC tag. The length field’s byte order differs from the surrounding little-endian framing.

The MAC covers version, IV, encoded length and ciphertext, excluding the outer frame/type and the trailing tag. A tag match gates AES-256-CBC decryption with BCrypt block padding; the resulting plaintext must begin with inner type `0x15`. The tag comparison exits on the first mismatch and is not constant-time.

A ready byte at B RVA `0x41C44` gates a 32-byte AES key at `0x41C48` and a separate 32-byte HMAC key at `0x41C68`. Analysis found reads of these globals but no initializer, setter or derivation. The handshake PSK was not shown to feed them. Unless another in-process component initializes this state, encrypted receive remains disabled. The [Launcher protocol](references/launcher-protocol.html) documents the key-state reads and the unresolved writer.

sections.title: PLK1 delivery and Core loading
sections.deck: PLK1 reconstruction is only the first gate: the Core must survive a protected cache save and reload before execution.

blocks.text: PLK1 validates the header, original and transferred size bounds, chunk sequence, optional raw-LZ4 decompression, and the final plaintext SHA-256. Both active callers request slot 0, corresponding to `PackClientCore.primary.dll`; no caller in this Launcher requests the secondary slot supported by shared code. The [PackClient Core analysis](references/core-analysis.html) follows this delivery through to the recovered DLL.

A fresh transfer is not loaded directly. `Save` must first persist the plaintext, then `TryLoad` must decrypt and re-hash the cached copy. Only the reloaded vector reaches `MemoryLoadLibraryEx`; successful network delivery alone is insufficient for execution.

Each of the eight complete historical transfers uses eleven ordered type-`0x15` chunks: ten carry 65,536 bytes and the final chunk carries 14,357 bytes. The resulting 669,717-byte raw-LZ4 object decompresses to the same 985,088-byte Core and matches the SHA-256 declared by the sender.

The cache resolves `CryptProtectData` and `CryptUnprotectData` dynamically and stores the Core by its plaintext SHA-256. This supports current-user DPAPI protection for the relative cache, although the absolute runtime base directory remains unresolved. The [Launcher protocol](references/launcher-protocol.html) traces the cache-hit and fresh-delivery paths.

sections.title: Inside PackClient Core
sections.deck: Historical PLK1 traffic reconstructs the Core and reveals its exports, transport, plugin system, updates, commands, and screenshot producer.

blocks.text: All eight complete PLK1 transfers—four in `260715-wd77daas7l` and four in `260716-dhnz7aft6z`—produce the same 985,088-byte x86 `PackClientCore.dll`, SHA-256 `4DE6EF8647FB4B599966A233740CB0514D1E71B8019A1A1792ED7E1E514EDF1C`. Across eight Core processes, all 352 retained mappings contain the same 753,664-byte `.text` section, SHA-256 `F06FF7AB6D62B761344CAECBCC6857912F7543F43C0E5FF462D2174BADB0CA3F`. The full-file and mapped-section hashes independently identify the recovered build.

Ghidra independently identifies the recovered payload as a little-endian 32-bit x86 Portable Executable and records the same full-file SHA-256 produced by PLK1 reconstruction. The complete identity and recovery steps appear in the [PackClient Core analysis](references/core-analysis.html).

### Runtime entry points

The DLL exposes 11 exports in four groups:

- Main entry modes: `Main`, `MainMinimal`, `MainWithConfig`, `RunWithConfig`, and `RunDualWithConfig`
- Launcher integration: `PackClientDll_AbiVersion`, `PackClientDll_Run`, and `PackClientDll_TrySystemSessionHandoff`
- Stored-plugin memory: `PackClient_AllocStoredPluginImageW` and `PackClient_FreeStoredPluginImage`
- Probe entry: `ProbeEntry`

`PackClientDll_Run` reads five fields from the Launcher's configuration block:

| Offset | Field |
|---:|---|
| `+0x00` | Host |
| `+0x04` | 16-bit port |
| `+0x08` | Group |
| `+0x0C` | Optional tag |
| `+0x10` | Optional configuration string |

The [PackClient Core analysis](references/core-analysis.html) traces the export preconditions and Launcher-to-Core ABI.

`RunWithConfig` starts one `S1` link, while `RunDualWithConfig` maintains separate `S1` and `S2` endpoint states. Core implements reconnect, heartbeat, and periodic DNS re-resolution and reads six local settings for fragmentation, DNS polling, TLS, application authentication, and preview control.

### Core transport and encryption

Core's authenticated type-`0x16` record uses a little-endian ciphertext length. A nonempty local `auth_psk` derives independent keys as `SHA256("PACKAPP|AES256|v1|" || raw_psk)` and `SHA256("PACKAPP|HMAC|v1|" || raw_psk)`; an empty value clears readiness and both keys. Core encrypts the complete original type and payload, then redispatches the decrypted inner record. The Launcher's earlier type-`0x16` envelope instead uses a big-endian length, unresolved key state, and accepts only inner type `0x15`. The [PackClient Core analysis](references/core-analysis.html) provides the complete application-envelope layout.

### Plugin loading and updates

The Core accepts a modern plugin ABI—`PackPlugin_GetAbiVersion`, `PackPlugin_GetFeatureId` and `PackPlugin_OnLoad`—and retains a legacy `Main` loader. Before dispatch, a candidate plugin must expose at least `RunWithConfig` or `Main`; the modern ABI adds further validation. The recovered implementation includes eleven feature-to-DLL mappings, screen-codec sidecars, staged raw-LZ4 delivery, legacy LZ4/zlib delivery, activation policy, and a paired current-user-DPAPI `.pblob`/JSON cache. The cache writes through a temporary file, flushes, atomically replaces the destination, and records feature, version, architecture, hash, size, and timestamps. It is separate from the Launcher's SHA-256-addressed Core cache.

Core updates use a distinct `CLIENTCOREUPD` path that stores DPAPI-protected chunks under `HKCU\Software\PackMonitorClient\LauncherDllStore\<bits>\Primary`. No plugin binary, paired cache, completed plugin delivery, activated mapping, or Core-update transaction appears in the available artifacts. The plugin and update paths are traced in the [PackClient Core analysis](references/core-analysis.html).

### Commands and capabilities

Beyond the observed startup and preview exchange, analysis identified handlers for:

- File, process, startup-item, scheduled-task, and registry operations
- Shell and payload execution
- Remote input, screen control, keylogging, and clipboard telemetry
- TCP and UDP proxying
- Virtual desktops and webcam handling
- Plugin delivery and Core updates

Captured traffic contains startup, inventory, offline-keylogger status, preview control, and screenshot delivery.

| Surface | Observed traffic | Recovered Core behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Session/startup | `INP HELLO`, `STARTUP PROBE` and `STARTUP OK` | Session/control router and startup-probe branch |
| Preview | Enable/request/ack exchanges and 15 `PV10` JPEG frames | GDI/WIC capture and `PV10` producer |
| Keylogger | `KTL OFFLINE` telemetry | Hook, archive, sync and clipboard-telemetry paths |
| Plugins | No transaction, cache pair or plugin bytes | Staged protocol, ABI, loader and DPAPI cache |
| Core update | No transaction | `CLIENTCOREUPD` validation and registry store |
| Auth envelope | No type-`0x16` frames | Optional Core KDF and AES-CBC/HMAC envelope |
| ETCHOOK | No activation traffic | Regex-controlled clipboard replacement |

The built-in preview producer uses GDI capture and scaling, `GetDIBits`, WIC JPEG encoding, and a bytewise `PV10` serializer. All 15 historical type-18 frames match that format. This path is distinct from the Launcher's raw-BGRX `1RCP` worker, and no recovered component bridges the two.

### Clipboard replacement

Core also implements regex-controlled ANSI and Unicode clipboard replacement through ETCHOOK. Proofpoint previously reported PackClient's clipboard-replacement capability; analysis of this build adds the built-in patterns and the concrete `PERCLIENT` and `SYNC` control formats. ETCHOOK does not appear in the captured traffic.

sections.title: Active-session handoff
sections.deck: Launcher B can relaunch into the active console session and replace itself when that session changes.

blocks.text:
The active-session path resolves a bootstrap executable, preserves a constrained set of special arguments, duplicates the current process token as a primary launch token and assigns it to the target console session before calling `CreateProcessAsUserW`. A separately selected user token can supply the environment; it is not the launch token. This is separate from the early screenshot mode, which exits through its own wrapper. Token selection and process creation are traced in the [active-session handoff analysis](references/active-session-handoff.html).

| Handoff detail | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Application and command line | Null application-name argument; mutable quoted command line |
| Environment | Optional Unicode block; handles are not inherited |
| Desktop | `WinSta0\Default` |
| Window state | Hidden with `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` |
| Creation flags | `CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB`, `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`, and `CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT` (`0x09000400`) |
| Retry behavior | Up to 30 attempts; each failure is followed by a one-second sleep |
| Drift check | Every 200 ms; a valid different console ID triggers replacement |

On successful drift replacement, the launcher closes child handles and exits the old process. It uses canonical `-acsi` state for this handoff. The continuity path is explicit in the Launcher, but the available runtime evidence does not identify which elevation API produced the original high-integrity host. The [handoff analysis](references/active-session-handoff.html) documents the drift state machine.

sections.title: Launcher B in process memory
sections.deck: Private executable mappings, a thread start, and Launcher-specific state connect the reconstructed image to the live surrogate.

blocks.text:
The first runtime capture preserves a bare 32-bit `SysWOW64\svchost.exe`, PID 5812, an NvSvc task, VMMap state, a user-mode dump and a late Process Monitor capture. The runtime correspondence below comes from passive examination of those artifacts.

VMMap’s 408 KiB private executable allocation at `0x002E0000` was an investigative lead. Its displayed “Thread Environment Block” label did not identify its contents. The dump’s package structure, embedded offsets, PE metadata and section hashes supplied that identification. [Samples and provenance](references/evidence.html) records the corresponding offsets and hashes.

| Runtime object | Location | Identification |
|---|---|---|
| Protected package allocation | `0x002E0000`; 417,792 bytes | Contains A and B at the expected logical-record offsets `0x128D` and `0x1CC1` |
| Mapped A | `0x02C70000`; image size `0x64000` | Entry RVA `0x1308`, timestamp `0x6A27AE4B`, and PE layout match the reconstruction |
| Mapped B | `0x05410000`; image size `0x48000` | Entry RVA `0x12FAC`, timestamp `0x6A3CB0B5`, and immutable sections match the reconstruction |
| Thread 1884 | Start `0x02C71308` | Start address resolves exactly to mapped A plus its entry RVA |

The complete protected allocation has SHA-256 `E49581067CC2AA5ABD09C8DF42D6FBD87CB064A9363FE8B52D8369FD1C51FFE5`; the embedded 415,071-byte logical record has SHA-256 `0419AE7381CAA97172C40F5AEA601B8A22F1F58D27F3930509AF5808E043F65E`. The mapped images are outside the registered module list. B-specific state includes the named mutant `PackClientLauncher.Session.9b2126fc5ed31443`, effective configuration, and formatted launcher diagnostics. Together, the package layout, mapped images, thread start, mutex, configuration, and diagnostics identify the live mapping as Launcher B.

No identifiable Core image appears in this local dump, although headerless content, missing pages, or a different capture moment cannot be excluded. The dump also does not reveal how the surrogate was populated. The [runtime analysis](references/runtime-analysis.html) combines it with cross-task Triage records that show the remote writes and `SetThreadContext` sequence.

sections.title: Persistence and execution modes
sections.deck: Process records connect the signed host to the surrogate and explain why full-EXE and direct-DLL execution produce different scheduled tasks.

blocks.text: During controlled execution in Windows 11, Process Monitor records successful loading of the adjacent helper after two earlier `0xC0000906` failures. A medium-integrity Tax Notice process, PID 5952, relaunches as high-integrity PID 2116. The elevated host creates the bare surrogate and the task-creation branch below. The session includes separate launch attempts; the process relationships are tied to their recorded creation events. See the [runtime analysis](references/runtime-analysis.html) for the native process evidence.

The relationship is specific: **svchost 3696 and schtasks 4600 are siblings under 2116**. Conhost 8248 belongs below schtasks. The parent exits shortly after creating its children; its continued appearance in a process tree preserves ancestry, not liveness. Later reuse of a numeric PID must be joined to a new process start and lifetime.

Native file and registry records establish installation beneath `C:\ProgramData\NVIDIA Corporation\NvSvc`, hidden and backdated copies, and HKCU Run/RunOnce writes in this chain. Task XML and the creation record establish NvSvc persistence. Task Scheduler shows the at-logon trigger, ProgramData action, and configured user context. The later capture also records the backdating operation rather than merely showing a timestamp mismatch. The underlying file, registry, and task identities are listed in [Samples and provenance](references/evidence.html).

Controlled Triage tasks close the apparent persistence discrepancy. Full-EXE execution copies and schedules `Tax_Notice_23665.exe`. Direct invocation as `rundll32.exe …nvdahelperremote.dll,#1` bypasses the expected signed host, so the carrier treats the sandbox host as its executable and persists a copied `rundll32.exe` without the DLL argument. That action cannot replay the original entry point.

“Highest privileges” here belongs to the selected current user; it does not mean SYSTEM. A later persisted-path launch is observed, but the saved local evidence does not resolve every trigger as logon versus on-demand. Across the Triage runs, remote writes followed by `SetThreadContext` on the suspended primary thread identify thread execution hijacking (`T1055.003`). The precise write primitive and installed instruction pointer remain unresolved.

A separate dump contains the 415,071-byte transformed package and a private mapping of Launcher B. After relocations and imported addresses are normalized, three package sites differ by eight bytes. This confirms that the package and Launcher were resident, but does not prove that the eight bytes form a port patch. Three `6666`-to-`443` substitutions would explain six bytes; resolving the remaining two requires the original before-and-after bytes from each site. See [Samples and provenance](references/evidence.html) for the recorded comparison.

sections.title: From failed connections to a live session
sections.deck: Local captures preserve failed connection attempts; July Triage traffic preserves the complete authenticated session and delivered Core.

blocks.text:
PID 5812’s preserved environment and formatted buffers identify `154[.]36[.]188[.]201:443`, a slot-0 pull attempt and `WSA=10060`. The PID 3696 set adds 373 ICMP host-unreachable messages quoting TCP SYNs to the same destination, plus two direct `SYN_SENT` socket views. These local artifacts establish attempted connections, not a completed session.

By contrast, the July Triage streams contain server PLC1, client PLA1, complete PLK1 delivery, and bidirectional Core traffic on the same TCP/443 endpoint. The September reruns `260908-zwr5naybjb` and `260909-abma8sab28` reached only the greeting/retry stage because the server returned no application data. The complete decoded sequence appears in the [PackClient Core analysis](references/core-analysis.html).

The packet capture has no PID metadata, so it cannot independently assign traffic to PID 3696; Process Explorer supplies that process-to-socket link. The successful July traffic uses TCP/443 but is raw PackClient rather than TLS or HTTPS. The preserved evidence establishes the different connection outcomes, but not why the server stopped responding. Capture identities and network observations are listed in [Samples and provenance](references/evidence.html).

sections.title: Analysis tools and detections
sections.deck: Offline decoders, a Wireshark dissector, and detection rules turn the recovered formats and behavior into practical research tools.

blocks.text:
Two offline Python tools and a phase-aware Wireshark Lua dissector accompany the analysis. They decode Launcher and Core framing, distinguish the two type-`0x16` formats, label observed Core messages, validate `PV10`, and export verified PLK1/Core and JPEG files when requested. Each export records its source flow, frame positions, size, and hash. All three tools operate passively on supplied files or byte streams. Setup and usage are described under [Analysis tools](references/tooling.html).

The test suite covers framing, authentication, both encryption formats, PLK1 reassembly and extraction, Core commands, `PV10`, capture reassembly, Wireshark integration, screenshot IPC, and detection rules. Running the tools against the historical captures reproduced the recovered Core and all 15 JPEG frames.

### Detection and hunting

The detection set covers three layers:

- Sigma rules target the observed `NvSvc` task, 32-bit surrogate creation, screenshot-worker mode, and active-session mode.
- Suricata rules include standalone Launcher markers that overlap existing Emerging Threats coverage, plus flow-aware challenge-to-PLK1 and Core-startup-to-`PV10` sequences.
- Separate YARA rules identify the recovered Launcher and Core.

On the retained case material, the Launcher rule matched all 86 Launcher mappings and none of 383 other objects. The Core rule matched the recovered DLL and all 352 Core mappings, with no matches among 116 Launcher or control allocations. A preliminary scan of more than 30,000 local Windows and installed-application PE files produced no matches for either rule.

The YARA rules remain experimental because they have not been measured against a broad enterprise-software or unrelated-malware corpus. See the [Detection guide](references/detection-guide.html) for rule logic, validation, and false-positive considerations.

sections.title: What this research adds
sections.deck: The recovered Launcher and Core extend the public PackClient account from campaign reporting into an execution and protocol reconstruction.

blocks.text:
Proofpoint’s 27 August 2026 report describes the Tax Notice chain, PackClient’s modular Launcher/Core architecture, representative protocol markers, and existing Emerging Threats coverage. Deception.Pro later documented PackClient hands-on-keyboard activity and ManageEngine use. This research adds the Launcher’s transport and loading contracts, direct Core reconstruction from PLK1 traffic, the signed-host/Donut/mapper chain, and working analysis and detection tools. [Proofpoint campaign report](https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/carry-compromise-ta4922-packs-packclient), [Deception.Pro later reporting](https://blog.deception.pro/blog/new-packclient-hok-aug2026)

Several pieces remain outside the recovered chain:

| Missing component or event | What would resolve it | What is known now |
|---|---|---|
| Plugin binaries | A preserved plugin transfer, cache pair, or post-activation memory image | Core contains the protocol, cache, ABI, and loaders, but no plugin PE was captured |
| Carrier write primitive | The precise write call site and the instruction pointer installed by `SetThreadContext` | Remote placement and primary-thread hijacking are established at runtime |
| External `1RCP` peer | The endpoint creator and type-2 consumer | Launcher B supplies the worker; no bridge to Core `PV10` was found |
| Real `1RCP` exchange | A complete READY/request/frame sequence from the malware worker | The code path and synthetic exchange agree, but the real exchange did not complete |
| Launcher envelope keys | The initializer or live values for the gated key globals | The receive format is recovered; its key source is not |
| Server implementation | Server-side code or configuration | Historical captures reveal behavior and commands, not the implementation |
| September non-response | Server-side telemetry or controlled infrastructure | The client sent PLH1 but received no application data |
| Production detector accuracy | Broader benign and unrelated-malware collections | The rules pass case-specific and local benign tests |

The [PackClient Core](references/core-analysis.html) note contains the full Core reconstruction. [Scope and limitations](references/limitations.html) collects the remaining technical gaps.

status: Launcher-to-Core execution, delivery, persistence, and C2 behavior
abstract: This report follows PackClient from its signed-host carrier into a suspended 32-bit surrogate, the injected Donut package, Launcher execution, and a 985,088-byte Core recovered directly from historical PLK1 traffic. Reassembled sessions preserve successful authentication, Core delivery, plaintext commands, and 15 PV10 JPEG frames. Analysis of the recovered Core reveals its plugin contracts, application encryption, update storage, clipboard replacement, and built-in screenshot producer.
key_findings: A 985,088-byte PackClientCore.dll was recovered directly from historical PLK1 traffic; its .text matches all 352 retained Core memory mappings.
A complete PLH1 -> PLC1 -> PLA1 -> PLK1 session continues into bidirectional Core traffic and 15 PV10 JPEG frames.
Normal full-EXE execution persists the Tax Notice host, while direct carrier-DLL execution produces a broken rundll32.exe task without the original DLL argument.
